🌍 Someone just open-sourced a Palantir-style global intelligence platform for free.

Palantir charges governments millions of dollars for software that tracks world events in real time.

Now, a developer named Elie has built an open-source alternative called World Monitor and released it on GitHub.

Here’s what it does:

A live 3D globe streaming data from 500+ news sources across 15 categories, with every update automatically summarized by AI.

It tracks everything from:

🪖 Military activity
💰 Economic shocks
🌪️ Natural disasters
💻 Cyber incidents
✈️ Flight traffic
🚢 Global shipping routes

You can also stack 56 interactive map layers to visualize different datasets at once. The platform calculates a real-time geopolitical stress index for 31 countries, updating as major events unfold.

It also monitors 29 global stock exchanges, commodities, and cryptocurrency markets from a single dashboard. It runs local AI with Ollama, meaning you don’t need an API key or cloud service to use its AI features.

World Monitor is available as a native desktop app for Windows, macOS, and Linux, supports 25 languages, and is designed to work almost immediately after installation.

A UK criminal gang has been sentenced after stealing over £4 million ($5.4M) in cryptocurrency from eight victims by posing as police officers.

The case highlights the growing use of authority impersonation in crypto-related fraud, where fake government and law enforcement identities are deployed to bypass victims' skepticism.

🔬 Capacity Deep-Dive #1: SOL/BTC (With Live Proof)

SOL is one of the most heavily traded assets on Earth, racking up $2.4 Billion in global volume over the last 24 hours. Because the SOL↔️BTC pair moves constantly across dozens of global venues, it represents textbook arbitrage. Every single micro-movement is an opportunity automated bots actively want to capture.

Theory is great, but production numbers are better. The GalaSwap SOL/BTC pool now exists, and because it is young and lean, it is performing exceptionally well.

### 📊 The Live Dashboard Snapshot (July 7)

GSOL / GWBTC (0.3% Fee Tier)

* Pool Depth: Just $26,000
* 30-Day Volume: $7.57 Million
* Daily Velocity: The pool turns over its entire depth ~9.5× every single day.
* Annualized Yield: ~262% APR *(based on yesterday's single-day fee snapshot).*

Let those numbers sink in: a tiny $26k pool routed $7.5M in a single month. This is the exact "early window" phenomenon in action—a small pool catching the full force of a massive, external arbitrage firehose.

---

### 📉 The Compression Curve In Action

As a pool grows and matures, its yield naturally stabilizes. You can see this live curve playing out right now across GalaSwap’s 0.3% fee tier pools:

* $26k Depth (SOL/BTC) ➡️ ~262% APR
* $160k Depth (SOL/ETH) ➡️ ~126% APR
* $866k Depth (BTC/ETH) ➡️ ~37% APR

This is our entire capacity thesis wrapped into three live data points: as liquidity depth grows, the rate cools. But notice how yields remain in the double digits even at nearly $1M in depth. Why? Because the volume is driven by external global market volatility, not by the size of our pool.

---

### 🚀 Where is the Ceiling?

How much liquidity can the SOL/BTC pool actually hold before compressing to ordinary DeFi rates?

The model indicates the ceiling is set by that massive $2.4B/day external market. Assuming a conservative 5% capture rate at the 0.3% fee tier, this single pool could productively absorb tens of millions of dollars in liquidity.

THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ CRISIS: Iran's Sovereignty Claim, the EU-GCC Response, and the Limits of Power
 
On 19 July 2026, the European Union and the Gulf Cooperation Council issued a joint statement rejecting any claims of sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz as "unlawful."
 
The message was direct: no bilateral arrangement between states may regulate or restrict the right of passage through an international strait. The right of passage, they declared, is guaranteed to all states under international law and "may not be subjected to the control or authorization of any state."
 
The timing was not coincidental. Iran had just suspended its commitments to the "Islamabad Memorandum," with Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi accusing the United States of violating the agreement. Tehran also launched ballistic missile and drone strikes on a U.S. base in Jordan. The suspension of the memorandum and the military strikes were simultaneous signals that Tehran would not be constrained by agreements it considered broken.
 
The institutional contrast is revealing. Iran's composite sovereignty score stands at 457.9/700 (65.4%) — political at 61.8/100, economic at 60.7/100, military at 72.5/100, and cultural at 77/100. Iran has the largest army in the Middle East — approximately 610,000 active personnel plus 350,000 reservists — produces over 900 types of its own weapons, and has no foreign military bases. Its defense industry exports drones and missiles to multiple countries.
 
Yet the Strait of Hormuz is not Iranian territory. It is an international waterway. Iran's claim to control it is a claim to control global energy flows — and the EU and GCC have now formally rejected that claim.
 
The paradox is structural. Iran possesses significant military and resource sovereignty — it has the third-largest oil reserves and second-largest gas reserves in the world. But its effort to project that sovereignty over an international strait has drawn a unified response from Europe and the Gulf. The EU-GCC statement explicitly rejected any attempt to "unlawfully regulate or restrict the right of passage through an international strait."
 
The question for the region: When a state with 457.9/700 sovereignty claims control over a global chokepoint, is it asserting sovereignty — or testing how far sovereignty can be stretched?
